utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Court Deputy, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready for your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the witness is ready. There is no need for any protective measures, as proposed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And could we have the witness, please. Well, by the way, Mr. Stojanovic, I've received the list of exhibits to be shown to the first witness and you did not indicate the status of those documents, whether they have already been admitted or not. And we see that there are some Prosecutor's documents' number there. Is it necessary for you to have your own number there? To us, so long as the document is admitted, the effect and the weight are same, no matter they're submitted by the Prosecution or by the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just for identification purposes we gave the Defence numbers, but these are exhibits which were obtained from the Prosecution, which means that finally, the already-given numbers to these exhibits will be used, the numbers under which these exhibits have been admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Dusko Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to spell your name because of the interpreters. Could you please spell your first name and last name.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: D-u-s-k-o V-u-k-o-t-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukotic. Could you please tell us your date of birth and where you were born.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 22nd of June, 1960 in the village of Trsic in the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, where did you grow up and where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I was born in a family of five and I went to elementary school, to the first four years of elementary school, in Trsic, where I was born. Two years of elementary school. After that, class 5 and 6, I completed in the village of Kozluk, which is also in the municipality of Zvornik in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 1972, my family moved to the village of Nikinci in the municipality of Ruma in the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina. That is in the territory of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, what's today known as Serbia and Montenegro. This is where I finished my high school. Actually, I completed the classes 7 and 8 of my elementary school in the village of Nikinci, then I went to the Stevan Puzic High School in Ruma, after which in 1979 I enrolled in the Faculty of Philosophy in Novi Sad, which I completed in 1974 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In 1984. Interpreter's correction, in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the Faculty of Philosophy" did you attend a special department or did you specialise in your studies at the Faculty of Philosophy?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The faculty includes several scientific groups and I graduated in the subject of philosophy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Once you completed your education did you immediately begin to work or did you continue to specialise in a different topic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Once I graduated at the Faculty of Philosophy, I gained the title of Professor of Philosophy and very soon I began to work in the same school which I attended -- in the same high school that I attended. I got a job in that same high school and also in another high school in Ruma, which is called Milenko Brzak Uca, and I taught philosophy and logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you work as a professor at school?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I worked as a professor very briefly, for only six months because already as a student I got married. In the third year of my studies, I -- me and my wife had a daughter. The salary of a professor was not enough to live normally, and there was a vacancy in the People's Army, in the newspaper or the bulletin of the former Yugoslav People's Army, whereby it was possible for those who completed universities and at the same time had already served in the army in certain branches and services could become professional soldiers after passing additional examinations. At the time, the Yugoslav People's Army offered certain benefits, so I applied for this vacancy, after which I underwent medical examinations and other tests, and in Banja Luka I went to the training centre for the mechanised and armoured units where I passed the tests and got the rank of lieutenant, so that I began my professional career in the former Yugoslav People's Army in 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that when you applied for this vacancy you had already served in the military, and in which service had you served, if so?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had already served my military term. I attended the school of reserve officers in the armoured units division in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that you had to be a reserve officer, was that one of the conditions in order for you to be able to apply for this vacancy?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now turn to your professional military career. So from 1986 you were a member of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do until 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: In September 1986 I was assigned as commander of the 1st Tank Platoon of the Tank Company as part of the armoured battalion in Ruma. I think after about a year spent in this job I was sent to Pozarevac, to the Guards Brigade, which was also an armoured guards brigade. I was sent to train as commander of a company where I stayed for three months, after which I returned to my home unit in Ruma and I returned to my duty as commander of the 1st Tank Platoon. In 1988, I -- this unit was actually transferred to Sremska Mitrovica to be a part of the 453rd Mechanised Brigade at the time. And in this 453rd Mechanised Brigade, I was appointed commander of a tank company. And as commander of the tank company, I stayed there until the 16th of August, 1992 when I joined the Zvornik Brigade in Bosnia and Herzegovina. By that time I already had the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us a little bit about how it came about that you transferred or came to Zvornik to the territory of the Zvornik Brigade and to join the Army of Republika Srpska, the VRS.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date exactly when the officers and younger officers, junior officers, non-commissioned officers from the 1st Army of the Yugoslav People's Army were called upon in Belgrade to attend a joint meeting at the Yugoslav army hall in Topcider. Combat operations at the time in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina were well underway. In view of the fact that in the former Yugoslav People's Army, following the events in Croatia, Slovenia, it was quite common for officers from the Yugoslav People's Army who were members of various ethnic groups mainly joined the composition of their newly formed national armies. So in the same way, we - members of the Serbian ethnic groups who were born in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina - received a similar call, which I responded to, because I received this call officially through my command, the command of the 453rd Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you for a second.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This call, was it received by officers who were born in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or was it also received by other officers who were not born in that area? I'm now speaking about that specific meeting at Topcider.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, at that time, that meeting, which was held in late July or early August 1992, was attended mostly by officers and NCOs who were born in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who conducted the meeting and how did it proceed, this meeting that you started to describe for us?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The meeting was attended by many senior officers. When I say "many," I think there were more than 300 of them, up to perhaps even 400. But there was no roll-call, so this is just my personal assessment that the meeting was attended by 3 to 4 hundred senior officers. The meeting was opened by someone from the command of the 1st Army of the JNA at the time. I really cannot remember who it was, of the officers. The meeting was attended -- we were introduced, actually, at the meeting to Mr. Ratko Mladic. I don't remember the rank he held at the time. I don't remember if he was major general or lieutenant general already. We were also introduced to Mr. Zdravko Tolimir. The meeting mostly consisted of a presentation of a military-expert view of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Mladic, on that day at that meeting, presented to us the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, certain areas of combat operations with emphasis on certain conflicts in certain areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he stressed at the time that in Bosnia and Herzegovina the Army of Republika Srpska which was just being formed at the time did not have enough expert personnel who could command under the concept of people under weapons and that that concept of the conflict. Perhaps I would make a mistake if I said that at the time there was an explicit order by Mr. Ratko Mladic for us to respond to this call, that we had to respond to the call and come to the Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I must say that at the time the command of the 1st Army was very cautious in issuing explicit orders about our participation and about our departure for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you at this point. Did you personally receive any direct order that you had to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina, or was it simply an appeal, a suggestion, a request?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, it was not a strict order that we had to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina. This led to a very poor response because as far as I can recall, out of that entire group, out of those 3 or 4 hundred officers, I think that on the 16th of August only about 60 officers went there with me, so that the response to this suggestion was poor. However, with the passage of time orders arrived, and in the meantime I did receive an official order about my stay in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what would have happened if you hadn't gone? Would there have been any consequences with regard to your professional career?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: It's hard to speculate about that now, but I think there would have been consequences because I know that for the most part officers who refused such orders did not remain in the army. I think that for each one of us our existential concern for our family - and I have to mention that in the meantime my wife and I had had another daughter - I didn't think about it much. I also have to point out that at that time I felt it to be my patriotic and professional duty to respond to the call of the people. I have to say, however, that with hindsight my opinion is that the evil would have been far greater had professional officers not taken part in the conflict among the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, as you understand, the character and the nature of the armed conflict is not the subject matter of this case and we are interested in what happened when the witness joined the Zvornik Brigade, especially during the critical period of 1995. Would you please pass this section and come directly to the subject matter of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This was my last question in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, we will now continue from the 16th of August, 1992, when you arrived in the Zvornik Brigade. Would you tell us briefly what you did on your arrival in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of August, with 60 other officers I arrived in Han Pijesak, where I was assigned to the Zvornik Brigade. I already then had the task of forming a reconnaissance sabotage unit whose first task would be to liberate the Zvornik-Drinjaca-Milici-Vlasenica communication, in view of the fact that at that time this was one of the main communications on the Sarajevo-Zvornik-Bijeljina route and it was unusable. Another route was being used which was extremely risky. As of the 19th of August, 1992, I assumed the duty -- I can't recall exactly what the title was at the time. I think I was the leader or commander of the Reconnaissance Sabotage Unit, and from the already-existing reconnaissance platoon and the already-existing sabotage platoon, I was to form a Reconnaissance Sabotage Platoon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Company - interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And these two units were to be melded into a larger unit and this was to become in fact a Reconnaissance Sabotage Detachment. Official orders arrived to this effect from the Main Staff through the Drina Corps, and these arrived in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us how long you performed the duty of commander of the 1st Reconnaissance Company, which then became a detachment.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I have to point out that while establishment-wise this larger unit was being formed, combat activities were going on. This was not purely theoretical work, but there were already certain combat activities going on. On the 31st of October, 1992 I was wounded in the village of Kitovnice, not far from Zvornik, and after my wounding I went for medical treatment and rehabilitation. I stayed there for about a month. On my return, I again assumed the duty of commander of the Reconnaissance Sabotage Detachment, because in the meantime it had been established and it was lined up in May 1993 on the FK Drina Football Stadium in Zvornik. There I reported to Mr. -- or rather, to General Milenko Zivanovic, who was then the commander of the Drina Corps. It was actually the commander of the Zvornik Brigade who reported to him, and I reported to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. I remained at that post for a very brief time, actually; until July 1993, I think. Another officer took over from me on that day and because of the consequences of my wounding - and this was causing me ever greater problems - I went to the brigade staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. This Podrinjski Detachment, the Reconnaissance and Sabotage Detachment; did it have a popular name, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: In establishment term, it was called the Podrinjski Detachment of Special Forces, but people referred to it as the Drina Wolves, because it was formed from the nucleus I have just mentioned, the corps I have just mentioned. And this name had already been used to describe the sabotage platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who at that time was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade? We are referring to the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: When the Podrinjski Detachment of Special Forces was being established in the form I have described and in the form in which I lined up the unit, the commander was already Mr. Vinko Pandurevic. I think at that time he was a major by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Vinko Pandurevic the commander of the brigade in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in 1993, who was the Chief of Staff and the deputy of the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think at that time, while I was commander of the Podrinjski Detachment of Special Forces, the Chief of Staff was already Mr. Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this duty of Chief of Staff and commander of the Zvornik Brigade, was it something he performed in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm certain about July 1995. I'm not so certain about July 1993, because in the Zvornik Brigade quite a few chiefs of staff took turns. So if I am mistaken, I hope it will not be held against me, because I really can't recall, but I think that Mr. Obrenovic was there in July 1993, and I'm certain he was there in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who took over from you as commander of the Podrinje Detachment?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The detachment popularly known as the Drina Wolves was taken over by Mr. Milan Jolovic as its commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this period - I am referring to the period up to 1995 - did you get to know Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you briefly tell us where you met him and how, and what duty he was performing at the time.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Dragan Jokic for the first time in the Vidikovac Hotel, which is located 2 kilometres or a kilometre and a half to the north -- or rather, to the south of Zvornik, where the Reconnaissance Platoon was quartered. And as I have described, later the Podrinje Detachment was formed from that unit. That is when we met for the first time, and I think at that time Mr. Jokic was the commanding officer in charge of this unit, which was quartered in this hotel. I think that he was training this unit at the time and looking after them, and this was the first time I met him. What his duty was establishment-wise and what his official title was establishment-wise, I'm not sure. I'm really not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point in the second half of 1992 did he perform the duty of chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: As I say, I must be cautious in making statements about who was performing what duty at that time. I think it's very likely he was already the chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade. He did hold that post in one period; I'm sure of that, but I'm not sure in what period. I am sure, however, that Mr. Jokic was Chief of Engineers in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall return to his position as Chief of Engineers, but allow me first to briefly go through your professional movements until July 1995. In 1993, in the second half of that year, you went to the command of the staff to the intelligence and security organ. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that at that time in the Zvornik Brigade the intelligence and security organ was a single organ?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No. The intelligence and security organ underwent certain stages of unified action and separate action. At that time I was the assistant of the Chief of Staff for Intelligence Matters, and this intelligence department had two officers, myself - at that time, I think I was a captain or a captain first class, I can't remember exactly - and I had a clerk. The security organ was a separate organ, but later on there was a brief period when this organ was unified, and then there was a third stage and that is the subject of my testimony today. And in that period it was again separate. To be quite precise: In 1993 when I was assigned to the brigade staff, at that point it was a separate organ. I was the assistant of the Chief of Staff, and Mr. Nikolic was then the Chief for Security, that is, the assistant of the Commander for Security. I remained at that post -- or rather, from that post, without changing my establishment post by an official order. I was sent to the area of the then - I think - I think 7th Infantry Battalion, because the battalions also changed their establishment names, so I will stick to the location to describe the units. I was sent to the village of Lokanj, to the Lokanj Battalion, and this was a little bit before the new year of 1994. I think it was in November, because at that time there were major offensives of the Teocani Brigade against the line of defence of our brigade, and at that time the battalion line was broken through and 14 soldiers of Republika Srpska were killed. These men had remained in the hands of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, just one second. I would like to ask the usher to show you a document. It's a document on the structure of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for identification purpose, Your Honour, this is a part of Mr. Richard Butler's report, Prosecution Exhibit P357 [sic]. And for identification purposes this is Defence 84/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, once you get this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, what's the number for the Prosecution's exhibit? I think something is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Prosecution Exhibit 367.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It has already been admitted into evidence, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is part of the evidence on the military events in Srebrenica from Mr. Richard Butler's report, so this is a segment from that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [Microphone not activated] Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, you have in front of you a document of the structure of the Zvornik Brigade in the relevant period in July 1995. Let us just briefly go through the document. At that time, who was the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: At the time the commander of the brigade is Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the Chief of Staff and the deputy of the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff and deputy commander to have brigade at the time was Major Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who is in the inner command?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The inner command is the commander, the Chief of Staff, or the deputy commander, the assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, could -- yes, we have put it on the ELMO. And I hope it could be blown up, since the words are very small. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will ask for it to be zoomed in to the maximum, because it's not very easily visible. And then we can confirm through this witness what is stated here. Could I please ask the technical -- the technicians to zoom in as much as possible so that we could see the positions in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may ask you for the transcript to repeat the answer to the last question, which was who constituted the inner command.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The inner command of the brigade comprised the following: The commander of the brigade, Mr. Vinko Pandurevic; the Chief of Staff and also the deputy commander of the brigade, Mr. Dragan Obrenovic; the assistant commander for security, Mr. Drago Nikolic; the assistant commander for morale and religious affairs, I think at that time that was Mr. Nenad Simic; and the assistant commander for logistics, Mr. Sreten Milosevic. I must emphasise - and I assume this is something that this Trial Chamber already knows - and that is that the command of the brigade depends on the kind of brigade that we're talking about. In this case we're talking about an infantry brigade, in view of the fact that there are different brigades than the commands and the staffs of those brigades are adapted to that and they can be different. In this case, this was the structure of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that these five people that we have termed as the inner command by establishment are practically above the officers in the staff of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in any case that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please help us. Could you explain the structure of the Zvornik Brigade Staff in July 1995. Who was at the head of the staff and, according to your recollection, who were the officers who were in the Zvornik Brigade Staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Please understand the following: The names and functions are something that I can speak about only in cases where I am sure. Why am I emphasising this? For the reason that there were very frequent changes on establishment posts. What I am sure of, though, is that in July 1995 the Chief of Staff of the brigade, Mr. Dragan Obrenovic, he was at that post. The chief for communications, who was also part of the staff -- even today I'm not sure whether this was Mr. Petrovic or Mr. Mico Jovicic. I'm not sure. But it was definitely one of those two, Petrovic or Mico Jovicic. The staff command commander - and I'm sure of that - was Mr. Milenko Jovanovic at that time. The assistant Chief of Intelligence was myself, Mr. Dusko Vukotic. The assistant for personnel affairs or the chief of the so-called personnel section was Mr. Mihajlo Galic, who spent the longest time at that post. The assistant for training and operations was Mr. Miro Dragutinovic. I cannot recall -- oh, yes. The Chief of Engineering was Mr. Dragan Jokic. Whether we had anyone in charge of artillery at that time, the chief of artillery, if we did have such a person, then it was Mr. Maksimovic, although it seems to me that at the time he was the commander and I cannot remember who was the chief at that function for the artillery. I also don't know if we had filled the establishment post of chief of the so-called PVO, anti-aircraft defence. I cannot remember that. I'm speaking - and I'm not looking at this diagram much because it's not very easy to see; and even if I could see it well - for example, I could see Milenko Kajtez here, but I'm not sure that in 1995 -- I mean, that officer was in the brigade, but I'm not sure that at that time, the time we're dealing with, he was actually at that post. So I'm not sure of that and I would not like to say whether he was or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a post in the staff structure of the commander or chief of the staff office or the staff command, as it is in the terminology of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I already said that the staff headquarters commander was Milenko Jovanovic. The staff command, the word itself, indicates that this was a kind of technical section providing administrative services, so I am not sure whether this is something that is considered as a formation. That is why I didn't mention it, even though we did have a staff office. We had soldiers and officers who were doing those duties, but I'm not sure whether that staff office is actually included in the structure of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These chiefs, the staff officers of the branches and the assistant chiefs, who were they directly subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: First of all, I can speak about myself, of course, and I can speak about general things from these military-expert regulations and rules, to the extent that I'm familiar with them and to the extent to which I understood the functioning of the staff. Generally speaking, it is clear that the Chief of Staff heads the staff, and that from the preamble and the attributes we were the assistants of the Chief of Staff in certain areas, and that in itself points to a certain degree of subordination. It points to who is managing and organising the work of the staff, who has the function to issue orders within the staff and who has the function to provide advisory functions, and who participates in certain sections of the work. So the precise answer to your question is that the Chief of Staff manages and organises -- manages the staff and organises the work of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now comment on your post, and then you can help us as much as you can about the Chief of the Engineering Service. So you were the assistant of the Chief of Staff for Intelligence Affairs.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any subordinated units that you were controlling and commanding in a certain sense, in a military-expert sense?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No. In that sense, at that point in time, no. In the military-expert sense, the concept -- the main concept and the military rules spoke about the Chief of Staff -- or the assistants of the Chief of Staff for Intelligence were to deal with the expert use and the expert training. They were supposed to work on the training and to propose to the Chief of Staff of the manner these units are supposed to be used, because according to military regulations the Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence, in his description of his duties, has the priority to secure combat operations in the -- from the intelligent aspect. And the intelligent securing of combat operations is carried out by the gathering of intelligence or information about the other side. And this gathering of information or data, as a rule, is carried out in several ways: It's done through reconnaissance; through sabotage activities; it's carried out by gathering data from the population, from the local population; it's carried out through electronic surveillance and anti-electronic activities; it is carried out by taking information or obtaining information from prisoners of war. These are all methods and ways in which the Assistant Chief of Staff, following the gathering and the checking of information, can influence the intelligence-securing of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me just to interrupt you for a second. You said amongst other things that the information you gathered also came from statements taken from prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is the level of the duties or responsibility or the attitude of the intelligent organ towards prisoners? Or more simply put: Who is responsible for the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The information -- the intelligence officer has the right only to take information, as far as prisoners of war are concerned; primarily, of course, this relates to information concerning the unit which the prisoner of war comes from, or all information that the prisoner of war can provide in order to secure their own combat operations, and this delineates the obligations of the intelligence officer towards the prisoners of war: care about his life, his provision of food, his status. All of those things provided under the Geneva Conventions is something that the security organs are in charge of. That's what they are responsible for. Specifically. I'm talking about general things. Securing prisoners of war or guarding them is the duty of the military police, which is under the security organ. Providing meals, food, hygiene, and that kind of care is indirectly the care of the logistics command. So the essence is -- to make it very simple -- is as follows: Their lives in any event are primarily under the care of the security organs and indirectly under the care of the logistics officers, the Assistant Commander for Logistics who is in charge of providing material supplies for his own unit, his own units, as well as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During that time, did you have the opportunity to use these methods to interview prisoners of war in order to gather information and intelligence about the enemy? You can say yes or no, because we will discuss this in more detail later.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just go back to this chart of the structure of the Zvornik Brigade. Below you there is the name of Milos Petrovic or Milos Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who that was, because later on he might crop up during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Petkovic Milos was a mobilised person who was in this organ before I arrived to the intelligence organ at the brigade command, and he was performing the duty of intelligence affairs clerk. At the time -- or during the stage when the intelligence security organ prior to this period was a single unit, at that time he also performed this same function. With my appointment as Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence, he continued to perform this work, even after the work of these two organs was separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that in the structure of the Zvornik Brigade the security organ in July 1995 was completely separate from the organ for intelligence affairs?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: This is an indisputable fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And only one more question, very briefly: The intelligence organ professionally, according to the hierarchy, was it also subordinate to the intelligence organs of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. All intelligence information -- or rather, all intelligence reports that were submitted to a superior, so the reports went up the chain of command and information went down the chain of command. Respecting this principle, the military rules provided for us as the Chief of Staff for Intelligence -- his duty was not only to provide intelligence for combat operations but also the intelligence officers in the brigade were directly subordinate to the so-called intelligence departments at the next level up. In this case, it was the intelligence department of the Drina Corps. To be quite precise and to explain this fully, the Assistant Chief of Staff, when assigned to the brigade, was in terms of discipline responsible to the Chief of Staff. He could not leave his post or go to perform any task without getting approval for this from the Chief of Staff. But as for his professional work, his professional instructions, he always had to consult, especially in more difficult cases -- when I say "more difficult," I mean the following: If an intelligence organ with respect to a source of information had to use an unusual source -- to be quite specific, if he wanted to collaborate with somebody from the enemy ranks -- he first had to get approval from his superior intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now focus on the Chief of Engineers. I understood that you said he was also a staff officer.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were the authorities and competencies of the Chief of Engineers and were they at the same level at the authorities and competencies of your service?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Chief of Engineers was primarily or was supposed to be an educated officer specialising in the engineers and Mr. Jokic, as far as I know, did have this training. I never talked to him about his education, but as far as I can tell he was educated in engineering and his knowledge of the professional convinced me that it was in fact his specialty. Analogously, he was also Assistant Chief of Staff, just like I was, and in the military and professional sense he was to advise the Chief of Staff with regard to his specialty. This did not mean that the Chief of Staff had to accept his advice as competent, but in principle that was what was envisioned, because no commander and no chief of staff can be familiar with every segment of military professionals. That is why there were various officers with various kinds of knowledge holding various posts who had an advisory role, because it was supposed that they knew their areas of expertise better than the chief of staff did. And in this mosaic of general knowledge before a decision was made, the chief of staff was supposed to hear out his assistants in order to be able to propose the most efficient solution in a given situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time - and I'm referring to July 1995 - was there an Engineers Company in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did it have its command structure at the time, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, like any company of any other purpose, it did have its own command structure. I think that at that time, whether it had a chain of command with a komandir, a deputy komandir and platoon leaders, well, I don't really know. I didn't go into that. But I do know that they had a company commander. I know that this establishment post was filled. I can't remember about the rest. So the answer to your question is yes; at that time the engineers did have an Engineers Company, which had its own commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Engineers Company, did he according to the rules actually command the Engineers Company?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: As a rule, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible in a situation of war, of combat operations and intensive fighting, the chief of staff or the brigade commander issues orders directly to the Engineers Company?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: In situations of war, especially in the situation we are referring to at this period, there was a lot of that, perhaps more than the regular use of units, because the military hierarchy at that point in time -- there was a principle of unity of command and the principle of subordination, but this could not be viewed ideally or typologically because chaos prevailed. There was chaos everywhere: In depth, at the front line, at the defence sector, at the point where there was contact between the BH army and the VRS army. There was a breakthrough by large numbers of soldiers. There were situations, the kind of situations that you describe, and there were many more of these than the rules would normally allow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to ask you briefly about Dragan Jokic, which is the reason we are here today. Can you describe for us his personality, his influence in the staff, his character, his position and the authority he held in the staff at that time, and his relations with the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, it's a compound question. It's so big, you know. And I understand that the witness is eager to give the evidence, but you have to take, well, lead, you know, to direct this witness to some specific answers. Let's deal with those, you know, questions one by one. We want you to put to the witness some questions in very concrete form.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, can you tell us what the position of Dragan Jokic as a person was in this staff structure in July 1995 and the following months.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I told you when I first met Dragan Jokic, and, of course, throughout these evil times which are now behind us, I formed a personal impression about this man, both as a professional and as a person. I feel that in the professional sense, regardless of his expertise and level of knowledge - because there is no doubt that he knew more than anyone else in the brigade about his specialty - I feel, however, that the attitude of his superiors towards him was never proportional to his knowledge. I never thought about why this was so, but to be quite specific, he did not enjoy any position of authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's just not responsive. Now he talks about the attitude of the superiors towards Mr. Jokic, which wasn't the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I quite understand that. Maybe that's the difference between the two legal systems, the common-law system and the civil-law legal system. And it's almost time for the break. And, Mr. Stojanovic, I hope that you could reorganise your question and ask some specific questions, one by one. And, Witness, during the break I hope you could think all those questions over. In this trial you have to be very responsive to the questions directly put to you. Most of the questions could be answered by simply saying yes or no. If the Defence counsel need more information, he will ask you some specific questions following up your answer. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. In my desire to assist the Court I felt it was important to say as much as possible. But I will respect your instructions. And of course, it's much easier for me to reply with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I quite understand that -- your eagerness to assist us is quite understandable. For instance, the last question the Defence counsel asked you is just about the position and the structure of Mr. Jokic in that brigade. And later on he will - I'm sure he will - ask you a question about your impression towards Mr. Jokic and his character. Then we'll follow up. Yes. Let's now take a break, and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, let us continue where we left off. I will ask you again to try to keep your responses as brief as possible, and I will try to direct you in your replies.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the system of work before this Tribunal. If you recall, we left off when talking about the position of Dragan Jokic in the staff of the Zvornik Brigade. I would like to know your opinion about the authority Dragan Jokic wielded in the staff of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Briefly, Dragan Jokic did not have any authority in the staff, but his subordinate liked him very well. He was well liked, both as a person and as a professional with expert knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say he did not have any authority, what do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I mean to say he did not participate sufficiently in the work of the staff and I think he was not esteemed by his superior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And who were his superior officers?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The chief of staff and the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in what way do you think he was not esteemed sufficiently or did not have enough authority?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Jokic, first of all, conditionally speaking, he was seen as an eccentric personality. He had his own lifestyle. He was a person who was quite retiring, who did not put himself forward, who did not care about leaving an impression as a professional soldier. He was not assertive. And also, he was not willing to suck up to his superiors so that what he said was not really taken into account sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that he did not manifest ambition, that he was not an ambitious man who wanted to advance in his career?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. We can view him in that way. Neither I -- nor, I think, my colleagues, but I'm referring primarily to my own impressions - I never felt that he was ambitious, that he wanted to reach high-ranking positions in the army, or that through his activities he expressed a desire to impress his superiors so as to advance in his career as soon as possible to get promotions or more important duties in the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was his attitude toward the authority of high-ranking officers, establishment-wise?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Establishment-wise I think that he tried to perform his work in the best possible way he knew, but he was not a person who would grab at jobs in order to focus attention on himself. So my impression was that he had a slight fear of authority, especially the superior command. I think that sometimes unfortunately he was prone to doing something ordered to him from the Superior Command which was not part of his sphere of duties and his area of work. I think he had some fear from the security organs. I'm not sure, but that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Compared to Dragan Jokic, the way you have just described him, what was Dragan Obrenovic's authority in the staff command?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic had considerable authority in the staff command, and he had every right to it, in view of his efforts, his diligence, and also his professional knowledge, because Dragan Obrenovic was an officer who throughout their military career, right from their training up until the performance of various officer duties, achieved very high results and had a pronounced professional ambition, which they achieved based on their work. And therefore he enjoyed a high -- he was held in high esteem by his subordinates as well as colleagues and his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the authority of Vinko Pandurevic in that sense? What kind of an officer was he?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: If I could grade these levels of authority, Vinko Pandurevic's authority was even greater than that of Dragan Obrenovic, of course, because of his formation, duty, and his rank also. Also, Vinko Pandurevic was graced with something that Dragan Obrenovic did not have, besides his military professional knowledge and skill. Vinko Pandurevic had a broadness which exceeded the specific military professional knowledge. He had a sense. First of all, he was very eloquent; he was a good speaker, which was captivating and gave the impression of a broadly educated officer. They were both brave, Pandurevic and Dragan Obrenovic. This is a characteristic that they shared. They were not just men of theory. But in the practical sense, in the period that we're talking about they were exceptionally brave officers. Of course, this is my personal impression and my experience of them. I have no intention of imposing my experiences and opinions as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the structure of the Zvornik Brigade Command, in the establishment sense, was the responsibility of the logistics -- Assistant Chief for Logistics, for Security and for Morale, was that above the position of the Assistant for Engineering?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: In the formation sense, if we're talking about assistant commanders, as the term itself says, the more formation duty of the assistant commander for security, assistant commander for logistics, defines these people as members of the inner command. Therefore, this is a superior formation position regardless of the rank that a certain officer at that duty has. So in brief, the answer to your question would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Due to their formation or establishment and the job that they were doing -- and when we're talking about Pandurevic and Obrenovic, did they enjoy more authority as officers than Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think that the answer would be yes, but the real answer could only be given by Mr. Pandurevic and Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukotic. Please allow me to move forward now and ask you to help us to understand the events relating to this period following the fall of Srebrenica. Can you remember when the preparations began for parts of the Zvornik Brigade to go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date when preparations began for departure for Srebrenica. I know that I did not take part in these preparations as a staff officer, and I don't know when the Zvornik Brigade units moved to the Srebrenica sector. I know when first information reached me about the capture of Srebrenica by the VRS, but the exact date of when the planning of this operation began and when the unit left for that area, I cannot remember. My only participation in this entire event is the specific task that I was given, just like I had been -- I had the task in similar operational situations, was to have my radio surveillance personnel to a location where this radio surveillance group can take part in the so-called repeater connection or relay, meaning that in places where you could not have tactical communication between the units via the so-called UKT devices or apparatus, where you could not have direct connections between two participants using hand-held devices, Motorolas, in view of this -- the fact that this unit had a stronger, more powerful repeater, it could relay information from one participant to another when they were unable to establish direct communication. So they participated actively in maintaining communications amongst our units. The other task was to use electronic surveillance and to record and note down conversations between participants of the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whom you sent there and when did you send them?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. The group usually left -- I'm speaking about experiences from other operations. They would usually leave together with the units that were leaving for the sector. They were leaving the seat of the brigade to the combat operations sector. Sometimes due to preparations, they would leave earlier. In this case, I cannot remember whether they left together with the rest of the brigade or if they left a day earlier. All I know is that -- I know that one of them was Milenko Panic, who from the beginning of the operation, from the beginning of his work to maintain the communications, as I explained, and who surveyed the enemy radio communications, Milenko Panic had the call sign of Premier, and I cannot remember who was there with him at the time, but I remember that the eavesdropping group included soldiers who gathered information in this way for me. I'm not talking about this specific group, but generally. At the same time, they were also assisting the Drina Special Operations Sector. We had Milenko Panic, Budimir Zekic, and there was another soldier whose name I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you properly that their call sign or their code name in that period of time when the Srebrenica events were taking place was Premier?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I must stress this was a group of soldiers which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not entirely clear what we are talking about. One of the questions before was: Can you remember whom you sent there and when did you send them? So it would be helpful to know what group is, are they sent to, what were they supposed to do. I'm not clear at this point. And now you're going into details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may, you know, ask some questions to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. We will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just go back. This group had the code name or the call sign Premier at the time.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did these soldiers belong to?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: They were in the establishment structure of the Podrinje Special Forces Sector. They were sabotage and reconnaissance units and they were below a detachment. However, in the sphere of information gathering, information about the enemy side were given to the commander -- their commander as well as to me as the assistant -- Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was their commander, the one that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Their commander was Milan Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Information about the enemy that they had gathered was supposed to be forwarded to whom?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The information about the enemy side was provided to the commander and to me as Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence. However, they also had direct communications with the brigade command, with the centre in the headquarters of the brigade, where from -- by telephone or wire communications they were able to report certain information directly to the duty operations officer or relay information if they felt that they were too sensitive from an intelligence point of view, so that the duty operations officer could find either the chief of staff or myself or the commander to whom they were directly subordinated. I'm now speak about situations where for any reasons they did not have secure communication at that point in time to be able to relay the information they needed to convey. I repeat: They could convey their information directly to the Chief of Staff and to the commander of the brigade if they were in the position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Vukotic, did you ever, as Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence, did you ever perform the function of duty operations officer in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the system, is the Assistant Commander for Security, was he ever in a position to perform the duty-operations-officer function?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was this listening post situated? What was the name of that location?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the location was at Mackov Kamen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this some mountain or a hill?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mackov Kamen is - it seems to me, I was never there myself - but I think that there is a repeater there -- there was a repeater there already and that there was a communications centre there. Geographically it was at such a distance and at such an elevation, to use the military language, from where it was possible to monitor the so-called tactical and even operational communications of the other side as well as of one's own units. When I'm talking about tactical communications, I'm thinking of short-wave communications, and -- which are followed by units of that tactical compositions. The other ones are the radio relay communications being maintained between the corps, brigades and so on between different corps, so amongst units of a higher level than those at the tactical level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point you said that this listening post could have direct communications with the centre at the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the purpose of clarity: Where was this radio centre of the Zvornik Brigade Command in that period, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you're speaking about the -- could you please clarify your question. Do you want me to say where the brigade radio centre was, the main brigade radio centre? The main radio centre of the brigade was at the actual headquarters of the brigade, at the Standard Barracks. I don't know. At the time I didn't -- I never went there. That communications centre was for a while at the Vratolomac Hill, but this is also very close to Standard. The soldiers that I am speaking about, they were not there; they were at a completely different location because the radio communications centre are subordinated to the communications chief, so they are part of the Communications Platoon, which is a brigade unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are now coming to the 11th of July. At that time, who was in command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: That's a difficult question, and I'll explain why. At that moment, as far as I was concerned, the commander was Vinko Pandurevic, speaking of the 11th. I do not have optical visibility with Vinko Pandurevic because he was in the barracks. As soon as I have no visibility with the naked eye, I don't know where he is; but I don't believe that already at that moment there was something on paper, an official order, as to who the brigade commander was. For my purposes, on the 11th the commander was Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where was Vinko Pandurevic on that day, to the best of your knowledge, on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: You have to believe me if I say that I don't -- I did not try to find out in particular. As a officer, as a subordinated commanding officer, you did not receive any reports as to where the commander was. There didn't seem to be any need for it. And even if he was dislocated to another place within the barracks, he did not feel it necessary to inform me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is the question is quite simple and he could have answered it in a brief way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I agree with you, but the witness already said at the beginning of his answer that it is a difficult question and I think we should allow the witness to explain why. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, you said that "it is a difficult question." Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Because the answer to this question has its normative stipulated aspect and a factual aspect. The legislative aspect is that there is a current valid order that the commander to have brigade is Vinko Pandurevic, whereas the factual situation means -- Who is the person who at that moment is responsible for the condition of the brigade? Since I have at that moment no information at which point Vinko Pandurevic is located, it is only logical that if he is not in the zone of responsibility of the brigade, his assistant or the Chief of Staff of the brigade performs the duties of brigade commander for that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we have received an answer to the question I wanted answered. Where were you, Mr. Vukotic, on that 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I know that I was in the zone of responsibility of the brigade. As far as I remember, I was either at the barracks maintaining communications with the units within the zone of responsibility of the brigade, because already then on the 11th I received information that combat operations in Srebrenica area had started and very few people, very few troops were actually within the zone of brigade responsibility. And I was working on the intelligence support of our units located in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. In other words, to be precise, I was probably working, as usual, on gathering intelligence on BH army units right across our defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very frequently during this trial we had opportunity to hear this term "zone of responsibility." I wanted to ask you: Is this a military term or the usual term that you use to denote the defence area of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Military terminology implies zone of responsibility, and that is a typically military term. The zone of responsibility has its left and right points and its depth. Depending on whether the brigade is in defence, it has a defence area. In this specific case, on the 11th, the zone of responsibility and the area of defence of the brigade coincided, with the proviso that one part of the units of the Zvornik Brigade engaged in the Srebrenica operation practically went beyond their zone of responsibility and beyond their defence area, which in military terms is certainly allowed. It goes without saying that the command may send certain parts of its brigade to take part in operations in various territories of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember where were you in the night between the 11th and the 12th?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I went to sleep in apartment number 10/3, Brace Jugovica Street, building B16, and I received a telephone call informing me about the fall of Srebrenica there, at home. The fall of Srebrenica is not exactly a military term, but it is certainly our military jargon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more precisely around what time it was and who called you.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: It was in the early-morning hours. It could have been 3.30 or 4.00 or 4.30 a.m. and it was soldier Milenko Panic who informed me, so-called Premier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you exactly on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: He asked me whether I was aware that Srebrenica had fallen. I said I was not, and it seemed illogical to me that I was being asked that question. And I said something to the effect, "You are supposed to know. You are up there." And he did indeed confirm that he had received such information, but he also warned me of one unusual circumstance: He said he had received information that the Army of Republika Srpska had entered Srebrenica, asking me at the same time whether I was aware or anybody else was aware of what was going on with the BH army troops around Srebrenica. Since my answer was negative, he put his Motorola against the receiver and I heard a terrible noise, a hum of -- in fact, a din of multiple conversations, like at a football match, and I realised the talking was among a huge number of people. It was in fact radio traffic among various participants. Since we always listened to each other in the course of gathering intelligence, just as we eavesdropped on the BH army -- we knew that they eavesdropped on us just as frequently -- and we did that so much and so often that we were by then able to recognise the voices of certain participants and their call signs. And listening that that din realised that there was a roll-call going on among various commanders of the BH army in the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After receiving that initial information, what steps did you take?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Just like any soldier, I suppose; I put on my uniform immediately and went to the command of the brigade to report to the Chief of Staff and report to him my latest information and what were then my assumptions as to what was going on. However, at the command of the brigade, the Chief of Staff was already informed of the fall of Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you for a second. Can you tell us approximately on the 12th, in the morning, when did you arrive at the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: It's really very difficult to give you the hour now, but I was a responsible soldier who took his job seriously, and if I received that call around 4.00, 4.30, I must have been at the brigade at 5.00, 5.30, because it took no more than half an hour from my home to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you say "Chief of Staff," you mean Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I then shared with him my assumption that a large group of BH army troops were probably setting off from Srebrenica to attempt to break through our lines towards Tuzla, taking the Srebrenica-Tuzla direction and Srebrenica-Kladanj. In my line of work, you tend to make assumptions based on the previous information you had about previous movements of the enemy side, because such movements had been taking place throughout the war in that area. But to confirm your assumptions, to be able to put them in an intelligence report you have to take into account a number of sources and determine the degree of truth you wish to present to your superior in the Drina Corps in the appropriate section.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "I supposed -- I assumed and informed the Chief of Staff of my assumptions that it was a large group," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Already in that first report I think I put down the number of 1.000 men, and the Chief of Staff, as I remember, asked me whether I thought perhaps that it was an exaggeration, that the number was too large. But being aware of the situation in the zone of responsibility of the brigade and the consequences of the weakened state of the brigade, in view of the fact that many of the easily manoeuvred and best-trained troops were already outside of the zone of responsibility of the brigade, I consciously exaggerated the number, perhaps so that the Chief of Staff could take appropriate steps to coordinate with the brigade commander who was out in the field, to reinforce the Zvornik Brigade in its own area of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the Chief of Staff, did you share this first information about the movements with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think I sent this information to the intelligence section of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, I would like to show this witness the map that was used by the Prosecution in interviewing Mr. Vukotic, and it would be useful for a more detailed explanation of Mr. Vukotic's movements. If you allow me, that's the centre of the map. I should like it placed on the ELMO. I think the place on the map is highlighted where Mr. Vukotic was located. It's in the centre of the map, and maybe we could zoom in on it on the overhead projector. The next sheet, please. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, after this first report and your conversation with Obrenovic, what was the direction of your movement?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: First of all, if I may ask kindly the Trial Chamber to bear in mind the time that has elapsed, nine years from the day when I gave statement to the Prosecution as opposed to two years ago. But I will try to describe my movements. My movement was motivated by the necessity to confirm my assumptions and the initial information I had received. First of all, you always try to envisage the possible consequences of your movements in a particular area of defence and zone of responsibility. So after reporting to the Chief of Staff and after sending this intelligence report to the intelligence section of the Drina Corps, I think I suggested to the Chief of Staff that we try to put together very quickly a temporary scouting group from the troops that had remained to come out into the field with me and try to confirm my assumptions. So as far as I remember, on that first day I went together with a group of soldiers to the area -- could we just shift the map a little here to try to find Velja Glava. It's a mountain chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could lower the overhead projector a little and move it to the left.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: A bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, you have a pointer. Could you please use it to indicate on the map that is on the ELMO so that Their Honours can see.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: We have to go to the south part of the map, because this area is towards the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, could you please show with the pointer on the map that is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The town of Kula is to the far right, but this is closer to the Kamenica area. I think that the Velja Glava mountain range is where we were. Why? First of all, because it's a very high elevation and it is possible to see with the naked eye the entire Kamenica Valley, to have an overview of it. And Velja Glava, which is very important, is a mountain range which conditionally speaking is at a safe distance from the line of defence of the Zvornik Brigade facing the units of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My fears, which I expressed to the Chief of Staff, related to the fact that the forces of the BH army on the Srebrenica-Tuzla axis had an empty area in depth where there were no units of the Zvornik Brigade, that there were quite a number of villages which were inhabited. And of course I went to reassure myself, to see whether this group was already breaking through and how far it had arrived. However, when we went up there, we saw no traces or anything that might indicate any movement by these forces and this led me to conclude -- not to mention, something that I have to point out, something that we have to bear in mind, the dynamics of these events, the radio surveillance was still going on. New information was constantly arriving. I was more and more convinced, I had more and more information from my surveillance group indicating that the participants in the radio communications which were very frequent were in the group that was setting out to break through. My information indicated that this group was most probably much larger than a thousand men and that's why I was convinced that from Velja Glava, from this mountain range, we would be able to observe this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you now look on the map.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the right-hand corner, upper right-hand corner you see an area marked in red. Is this where you were approximately?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is Velja Glava. This is the Velja Glava mountain range. And you can see in front of it there is a valley. You can see the elevations marked here. And you can see the valley where we were able to observe any possible movement. And then you can see the area of Kamenica. All this was for the most part an area that was completely empty of our units. Should I take this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could only use the pointer to indicate the area of Gornja Kamenica that you are referring to. But please, on the map that is on the ELMO, Mr. Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the whole area from Velja Glava, this entire area from Velja Glava all the way here, which is the depth of the brigade, including the mouth of the River Drinjaca, which I can't find here at the moment; also, the communication from Drinjaca towards Konjevic Polje and Milici, even Konjevic Polje itself. All this was an area where there were no units of the Army of Republika Srpska, except that in this area there were certain villages which were inhabited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After you had failed to observe any members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you returned to the brigade. Who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think I returned to the brigade, but of course I was still doing my job. I was still gathering information and looking for ways to fully confirm and complete the intelligence information, wondering how to get this information. I think that on that same day I received from the Chief of Staff, Mr. Obrenovic, information to the effect that in the area of the then, I think, 4th Battalion in Kajici - that was where its command was - in the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade, that a prisoner had been taken and that he was to be interviewed. I got into a vehicle - I don't know exactly who went with me - and I went to the area of Kajici. And I think that there was a forward command post in Jezestica. I went there, but I did not find the battalion commander, because according to what the men who were there told me, he was on the ground with his unit and there had already been an exchange of fire between the group breaking through and the forces of -- I think it was the 4th Infantry Battalion at the time, which had been attached from the Zvornik Brigade to the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade. In answer to my question as to whether it was true that they had a prisoner, I was told that this information was not correct, that they had had a prisoner but that allegedly - at least according to what they said - he had attempted to flee and that he was no longer alive. I have to say that I saw neither the prisoner nor anything else. This was the information I received. I returned from there to the area of responsibility, but on my way back through Konjevic Polje to the brigade command, I could hear heavy gunfire in the area, where the Milici Brigade and Bratunac Brigade met up and in the area of responsibility of our battalion, which had been attached to the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
