utterances.text: Travelling along this asphalt road in the direction of Konjevic Polje and Drinjaca, did you observe any policemen or members of special police units?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't observe anything special, except that in the school in Konjevic Polje, where an engineers unit was usually quartered which was part of the Drina Corps, you could see some commotion. However, this was logical because you could hear the fire very well. But I didn't notice anything special. I didn't even notice any traffic or anyone travelling along the road -- or rather, I didn't notice anything special on the road. The traffic was quite normal. It could have been 11.00 or 12.00, noon, or maybe in the early afternoon, but there was nothing unusual going on except for the gunfire which could be heard some way off from the road. It was evidently the forces of the BH army and Republika Srpska who were already firing on each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you got back to the barracks, who did you inform of the fact that the prisoner you were supposed to interview had been killed in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I informed the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he in the command at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think he was. If he wasn't, he was nearby; he was somewhere in the area of responsibility. I can't remember whether he was in his office or somewhere in the compound, but I did inform him that I had been unable to check our information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that information was coming in on a daily basis. In the evening of the 12th, was there any new information about the size and movements of the column?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff and I were still checking the information from the field at my suggestion, and I think that on that same day we sent a group again to the Dzevanje or Jesenje area. These are villages from which one can see the Drina River Valley and the area below Gludas. You can see Glodi. You can see this on the map on the upper right-hand corner. Because across the river there is a bridge there, and we knew this from before because units often took that direction when breaking through toward Tuzla. That's why I again sent a so-called temporary reconnaissance group. As far as I can remember, they were led by Jasikovac, by Lieutenant Jasikovac, who took them up there to check this information. I insisted with the brigade -- with the Chief of Staff, that is, that they should keep a safe distance because all the information that was coming in indicated that the number of members of the Army of BH was enormous. They had come out from Srebrenica and were breaking through in the direction of Tuzla and Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask the usher to assist me in showing the witness the next document. For purposes of identification, Your Honours, this is Exhibit P452 and our identification number is D92/3. This is an intelligence report which our witness compiled on that day, at least according to the text and the signature. I will ask that the English text be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, do you recognise this text and do you recognise the signature at the end of the text?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No. This was handwritten by my intelligence clerk, Mr. Milos Petkovic. This is his handwriting. But I confirm the veracity of this text. It is probably due to other things I had to do that I told him what to write and I just signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you just tell us what the date is in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The 12th of July, 1995. This is an intelligence report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please read us the stamp at the end showing when this report was sent to the command of the Drina Corps. If you can assist us, when was this sent? And this is stated in the seal.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think that according to what it says the report was sent off on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What time?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: 01.10 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So immediately after midnight, between the 12th and the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to go through this document with you. According to this report, to whom are you sending this intelligence information which you received in the night between the 12th and the 13th?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The procedure was the following: Besides the oral report that I submitted to the Chief of Staff, there always had to be a written report, which is why this was written down. And this had to be given to the encryption service and they forwarded it to the command of the Drina Corps, the intelligence organ, as is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say at one point: "According to information received at 1900 hours you thought that the column was then in the area of Velja Glava and was on its way to the Spreca River Valley." Is this what you were telling us just a minute ago, the intelligence information you had?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You heard me talking about what I had done during the day, but by the time this report was sent off, the information had been checked because the temporary reconnaissance group led by Mr. Jasikovac, in the area of Lisanj, had already observed a huge group of members of the BH army which had just passed through Glodi and was on its way through to the area of Velja Glava, just as is stated in this report. But one should bear in mind the following: This enormous group of men is a drawn-out column, so some were in one area and then there were stragglers 2 or 3 kilometres behind them. Information that was received later on indicated that this was a typical combat disposition. So in military terms, this was a column that was respecting certain military rules. It had its reconnaissance; it had its flanks; it had its rear, so it cannot be viewed as the static category. If you mention Velja Glava, it doesn't mean that at that point they were all at Velja Glava.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Allow me now just to comment on the sentence before the last, where you make the conclusion: "I estimate that the defence line from Baljkovica on the right is threatened." Is this the direction in which the column actually moved in the following few days?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And it is in this region that the main thrust from the rear of the Zvornik Brigade took place, and this is where the most fierce fighting took place in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now talk about the night between the 12th and the 13th. Can you tell us very briefly what your movements were on that day, between the 13th and the 14th in the night.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure now. I think that in the night between the 12th and the 13th - I'm not completely sure; I think it was between the 12th and the 13th - based on information which had already been checked and verified, the Chief of Staff took units of different specialties conditionally speaking, units from the rear, communications units, and parts of engineers units and so on, and tried to put together or did put together a temporary group to go to the Snagovo area, because to go to the mountain range from which it was much safer to protect the rear of our units, at the first line of defence, this was already too late because parts of the units had already broken through and passed over that mountain range. And then when we talk of the Karakaj-Caparde- Sekovici communication, which might have been a stronghold, because crossing that road meant a total delay in organising the defence of the brigade area. And I think that I was there and that the Chief of Staff was there. We went there late at night, at about 1.00, where there was a tank, a self-propelled weapon, a Praga, but I'm not sure whether it was between the 12th and the 13th or the 13th and the 14th, but I think it was the 12th and the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how many soldiers or members of the Zvornik Brigade units assembled in this way went to the position.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: In terms of military strength, it was not very significant. First of all, besides the tank crews or one of the self-propelled gun or Praga crews, the rest were either logistics or engineers units members who don't have specific experience in a typical military combat in the field, and I think that according to the order of the Chief of Staff a part came from the Kiseljak Battalion. They were, let's say, younger and more experienced soldiers who at that time were not in the Srebrenica sector, so they joined us in order to form a smaller group to attempt to stop the column so that it would not come to the rear of our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those days - on the 12th, on the 13th - did you have an opportunity to speak with or to see Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those two days, on the 12th and the 13th, did you have information that practically Obrenovic was conducting the defence of the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: In the normative sense, Vinko Pandurevic was still the commander, but practically the person who issued orders to everybody in the area of responsibility was the Chief of Staff, Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever during those two days, on the 12th or the 13th, see Dragan Jokic anywhere?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So now we come to the among to the 13th. You spent the night at Snagovo. What happened then, Mr. Vukotic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Since the situation on the ground was much clearer now, certain information was arriving from the local population, from the villagers that -- of villages that I mentioned who were in the depth of the brigade's area of responsibility. Various information was beginning to come in about a long column and the combat disposition -- its combat disposition, which was moving towards Tuzla and Kladanj. The situation was much clearer, and because of that there was a new aspect now. I was becoming concerned about the following - and I spoke about this with Mr. Obrenovic - and that was that there was a possibility that the forces of the B and H army go to Razvorni [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far were the forces away from Zvornik at that point?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: A part of the column was practically not more than 1.5 kilometres as the crow flies away. Again, I would like to say that this was a very large group of people and that my intelligence assumption in which I was speaking about 1.000 people, it turned out that I underestimated the strength of this group. As it turned out there were actually 15.000 men there. Again, I say such a large number of people in a column, in a military sense, with their reconnaissance rear section, were deployed over a large area of people from Mountain Udrc practically, which was more in the area of responsibility of the Vlasenica, Miletici and Zvornik Brigade, at a depth which -- and the front area which had already arrived at the section of Maricici, practically below Snagovo, which was only 1 kilometre or 1.5 kilometres as the crow flies away. I think that we could look at this picture. We could see that the combat disposition was deployed over a large area. I assessed that this could be quite dangerous for the town of Zvornik, so I proposed to the Chief of Staff that he should urgently inform the command brigade -- the brigade command so that the manoeuvring forces would be returned as soon as possible to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you on the 13th in the morning and in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic - after my assumptions and after the information which I kept forwarding to him about what was going on - he sent me to Kula, to the town of Kula. This is a place above the town of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: To the location of Kula, which is a situation -- a location above Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where I was able to have good radio communications and at the same time from that area we knew that we had to concentrate our forces up there because that was the best position for a possible defence in order to prevent them from entering the town of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that at that point there was a distance of 1.5 or 1 kilometre as the crow flies between the front of the column and the town of Zvornik and that in between there were no serious military or police structures from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, in the morning, practically there was nobody there. The town was living its normal lives. The lives to have citizens were proceeding as usual, with the exception that the male members of the population who were of military age, were deployed to their military tasks. Practically there was nobody there, except for parts of the police which need to be stationed -- except for the police, which were stationed in the town of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I was just hoping that we could take a break, Mr. President. And just to clarify. I believe he's speaking of the area of Kula which is south of Zvornik, not to be confused with the town of Kula which is north of Zvornik near Pilica. And since these will be important in the future, I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe Mr. Stojanovic could ask some questions to this effect after the break. But frankly speaking, Mr. Stojanovic, I see little relevance of the testimony of this witness, you know. The issue is that we want to know the day-to-day practice of your client, Mr. Jokic, but not this witness. If the testimony of this witness, of his daily work, has to do something with your client, which we believe is the relevant, but up to now I do not see that. And I hope after the break you could give the witness some guidance in that direction. Yes. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, before you start, would you please tell me how long your direct examination will last for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The way I have organised my questions, I believe that we will probably finish the examination-in-chief of this witness today. I spoke with Mr. Waespi and Mr. Karnavas also during the break about the time they require, because in our estimate we planned to complete the testimony of this witness in two days. They said that they didn't need as much time as I did for my examination-in-chief, so I believe that we will not have a problem with the scheduling. Also, allow me to apologise because I wished through this witness to present a general context of the events in Zvornik over those few days, and I would like to assure you that the future witnesses will not dwell in such detail on these events. We would like to use the presence of this witness, however, to make certain points about our case. And thank you very much for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the information. I think this is your first witness and the Bench will give you some leeway, you know, to ask some more questions. But still, we hope you could finish your direct examination today. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, I hope you had a rest during the break, and please allow me to deal with this dilemma brought up by Mr. McCloskey. In this case here we frequently mention the toponym Kula, indicating the Kula school in Branjevo. Today you used the same toponym to indicate the town of Kula. If you can help us, please, we will look at the map. We have now focussed on the location of the town of Kula. So could you please specify where you were on that date between the 13th and the 14th. I would also like to clarify that this map was given the number D128/3 for purposes of identification. Please go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I understood your question, just like the Prosecution stated, this is the toponym Kula Grad. It's a location above Zvornik, and it's circled here on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take the pointer and indicate on your right where this is. Could you please point not on your screen but on the map itself.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I am now pointing to the town of Zvornik, and then I have moved the pointer to the place where I was on the 13th, the location called Kula Grad, which is in the immediate vicinity of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is what I wanted you to help us with. And we will keep to this part of the map. On the evening of the 13th to the 14th, were there any clashes with this incoming column? Was there any fire exchanged with the column?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes. The first firing encounter with the incoming column occurred in the region of Djafin Kamen, the broader area of Velja Glava where our temporary pioneers unit was located, which was commanded by a military police officer, Aleksandar Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately when this first contact took place between members of the Zvornik Brigade and the incoming column.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think this happened around 21 or 22 hundred hours on the 13th. Since I had a radio connection with them during which Kostic informed me about this exchange of fire, I assessed that this small temporary scout group was in danger up there, and I suggested to the Chief of Staff via radio -- I actually sought his permission to pull out this scout group from that sector and this is what was actually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were in communication with the Chief of Staff via radio.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is an important question for us, I would like you to explain what radio communications you had with the Chief of Staff at the time. How did this communication function?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I had a dual radio communication with the Chief of Staff. We were in communication with short wave via Motorolas, and also I had another device. It was an RUP radio device, so that I had a parallel communication. The Motorola was mine, I had it, while the communication via the RUP device was maintained via one soldier who was given to me by the Chief of Staff, who was with me at all times and who conveyed information to the Chief of Staff or I would directly take the device and report on this other line of communication. Because experience showed that short waves could be monitored very easily, whereas the RUP could also be listened to, but it was a little more difficult to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To make it absolutely clear, where did you have the RUP-12? Was that in the possession of a soldier who was accompanying you at all times?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I did not have a directly subordinated soldier, so it wasn't a soldier who was subordinated to me. I think he was attached to a mix artillery division which served this RUP and which hand to be next to me on Kula Grad, because at the time on the 13th, already during day police units began to group and some temporary military units also began to group in order to protect the town, as I described in my testimony before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So to understand that period from the 13th to the 14th, you were at Kula Grad. You had a soldier who was attached to you, a communications soldier who had an RUP-12 device with him.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were in communication with the Chief of Staff but you also had a Motorola using short waves through which you were in communication with the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day -- on those days, the 13th, 14th, 15th, did you have any direct radio communication with the brigade and the duty officer at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No. In all the days that I spent in Kula Grad in that whole period, I had radio communications directly with the Chief of Staff and occasionally with the eavesdropping group that I mentioned, plus another eavesdropping group at Gucevo, and that other group had different call signs on different days in the radio network. I think they responded to the sign of Drina and possibly also "Premier" was used by them as well. Premier communicated from the point I mentioned earlier, and the point I'm mentioning now. I could not make a mistake as to who was calling from where, because I was very familiar with the modulation of the operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in concluding that on the 14th you had absolutely no direct communication with the duty officer at the brigade whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Not only on the 14th. I didn't have any direct communication with the duty operations officer or with the communications centre stationed at the barracks at any point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard Mr. Obrenovic testifying here, and we are aware of his interview where he said that on that day he had had communication with you but only one-way communication, meaning only short-wave radio, not through the field radio RUP-12. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I am certain that I had two-way communication, both by short-wave radio and the other kind of radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So Obrenovic would not be right in saying that you only had short wave radio communication?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us try to clarify, in view of the exhibit that we are going to see very soon. When do you use the short wave communication and when do you opt for the RUP-12?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I usually use short wave communication when I am transmitting information of a lower degree of confidentiality, and I always use it if at that moment the Chief of Staff is in a position to hear me. There is a possibility that he hears me frequently, but due to his other obligations in the field he does not always respond. He obviously -- in fact, it would be wrong to say "obviously," because I do not see Mr. Obrenovic, I don't have visibility -- but most probably Obrenovic has an operator of the RUP field radio with him. And when I don't have confirmation from the Chief of Staff that my information has reached him, I turn to the other field radio RUP and transmit the same information again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on that communication that you had with Obrenovic, were you able to locate him precisely?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No. It would be preposterous to claim that you can locate somebody based on radio communication, because in view of the point where I was located you can communicate from that point also with a Motorola in a range of 60 to 70 kilometres depending on the terrain, so you are certainly unable to determine the location of the co-locutor based on the radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, with the assistance of the usher I would like to show the witness one intercept, marked for identification 452 by the Prosecution, and our identification number is D92/3. The intercept dates back to the 14th of July. The co-locutors are Zivanovic and Jokic at 10.10 hours [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think there may be a mistake on numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe it's Prosecution Exhibit P227 and your internal D exhibit D100/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. Thank you, Mr. Waespi. So our exhibit is 100/3, and it's Prosecution Exhibit D227. And my colleague has just informed me that the time recorded in the transcript is wrong. This intercept was marked as having taken place at 0910 hours, not 1010. Just for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vukotic, we have had occasion here to work with intercepts including this one, wherein the BH operator located in the territory of the 2nd Corps of the BH army identified Milenko Zivanovic and Major Jokic. I will comment on a part of this intercept. The participant recorded as Jokic is informing the corps commander and says: "They were crushed up there on Velja Glava," meaning the column, "and a huge group is moving towards the Drina according to intelligence, towards Zljebac Mladjevac. The group is huge, absolutely enormous. Terrifyingly huge." Commander Zivanovic says, "How big is the group?" And the participant identified as Jokic says, "It's huge. Ever since I heard this information, I can't fucking believe it." And the participant identified as Zivanovic asks, "Who told you that?" Participant Jokic answers, "Thousands of them. Our intelligence officer sent us an info." Question: "Which intelligence officer?" Answer: "Dusko Vukotic." Question: "Where are you calling from now?" Answer: "From here. From --" and then there is a pause. "As a duty officer." Now, this comes -- here comes a part of the conversation where I have a question. You told us a moment ago that you had no direct communication with the duty operations officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that on the 14th in the morning you did not give any information about the size of the column to the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first part of this answer, it says -- the person identified as Jokic, "They are spread out from Velja Glava and they are moving towards the Drina." Did you have any operative intelligence that this large group was spread out at Velja Glava or crushed?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that there was a fire exchange between them and the temporary scouts group, and it is logical and most probable that this group attempting a breakthrough had no information as to where our forces were waiting for them. And it's quite logical that in that situation the column would be seized by panic and spread out. What you just quoted seems to corroborate what I just said about the towns being in jeopardy. Mladjevac and Zjlepce are elevations right next to the road, the road that was currently in use. You could use it to travel from Zvornik to Drinjaca, and Mladjevac is right next to Kula Grad, where I was. From this intercept we can draw the conclusion from Jokic's words, where he says that "They got this information from the intelligence officer," meaning me; however, from my location, my written reports that were forwarded to the corps command were written in hand and sent by me to the encoding officer, to the encoding centre, showing them beforehand to the Chief of Staff so that the Chief of Staff could coordinate work and operation in the field based on that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely something I wanted to ask you about. Who would then in the system of communication be the person who could give this information to the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The duty operations officer could possibly get this information at a time when the Chief of Staff is absent by the soldier carrying it, because the soldier who was carrying this piece of paper -- even before taking it to the encoding centre to be forwarded up the chain of command to the Drina Corps knows that the Chief of Staff needs it anyway for operative work. And if the Chief of Staff happens to be absent at the moment then the soldier could give it to the duty operations officer first so that the duty operations officer could inform the Chief of Staff and thus enable him to take appropriate steps in the further course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that the Chief of Staff is the hub of communication and coordination of all the actions and information within the zone of responsibility of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so, because -- practically, it should be the commander of the brigade. The brigade commander has intelligence and every other responsibility in the zone of responsibility, if he is there. If he is not in the zone of responsibility, what you just referred to in your question would be the responsibility of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're talking about 9.00 on the 14th. Do you know where the Chief of Staff was at that moment?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No. No. I did not know the whereabouts of any of the commanding officers at that point, because - and I want to stress this again - I was unable to determine the location of my commanding officers with whom I had communication just based on our radio exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is an indubitable fact that the duty operations officer was aware of this information that you forwarded to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: At that moment I didn't know it, but we see now that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we infer from this that the Chief of Staff had conveyed this information to the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Look, the Chief of Staff did not need to, was not required to - in principle or otherwise - to inform the duty officer. He could have perhaps tasked the duty officer to work as a messenger and forward this to the superior command. And I do not wish to denigrate the responsibilities of the duty officer, but it's only natural that if he's unable to communicate with the operative command he will convey the information to the duty operations officer to be forwarded to the superior command, because once you write the written intelligence report, it doesn't mean that having travelled the entire chain of command through proper procedure it will reach the recipient in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, let us clarify one thing: This information about the movements of the column were in the hands of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Since I was sending from Kula to him, it would be logical that the information travelled to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to take you back to your own movements. You said you were in Kula Grad in the night between the 13th and the 14th.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the course of your activities on the 14th of July, the movement of that column, and all that was going on.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: All my activities were essentially focussed on gathering information and making estimates on the possible danger to the town and the Zvornik Brigade, since there were no commanding officers which according to establishment would be in charge of linking up units in this area. And since I as Assistant Chief of Staff was already in Kula at the time when police units had begun to arrive, at a time when parts of certain combat units of the VRS from the Zvornik Brigade had started to arrive, having been pulled out from certain defence areas of their own, I was helping to brief them on the whereabouts of our units that were supposed to defend the town of Zvornik and the road Karakaj-Caparde- Sekovici, because I already had an idea based on the information I was forwarding, including information from the Chief of Staff saying "Our units are arriving. Show them where our men are so as to avoid friendly fire." And then if a commander leading the police unit would come to see me, I would tell him, "In this area of Marici [phoen] you should find a unit from the VRS." But my priority task, my foremost task was to monitor the operation in the field of this military column that is the subject of our conversation and to try to gather intelligence on the movements of the BH army forces in front of our first-defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time learn about the activities of the 2nd Corps of the Army of BH in the direction of the Zvornik defence lines and a possible breakthrough through those lines?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I was convinced that there was communication between the command of the 2nd Corps of the BH army and the members of the 28th Division and that while the column was moving, there was communication. It's possible that due to the circumstances I have spoken about, the fact that the column was drawn out, there was no communication with some parts of the column, and I am quite convinced that there was no communication with the head of the column. But the fact that there was communication with parts of the column was confirmed to me by members of the surveillance groups. I was convinced that members of the 2nd Corps of the BH army were intensifying their activities and the pressure on the line of defence of the Zvornik Brigade. This led me to the conclusions that this was a coordinated operation by the column breaking through and the BH army forces in front of the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. Our greatest fear was that in case there was an incursion by the forces from the column into the town of Zvornik, total chaos would ensue, and our forces would retreat from the line of defence because everybody would go home to defend his family in the town without thinking about the area of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at some point learn about a breakthrough by a unit headed by Naser Oric into the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember whether I submitted a written report on this, but I am sure that the information reached the Chief of Staff from me that Naser Oric with a part of the men was already in the depth of the area of defence of our brigade; that is, that a reconnaissance sabotage group had been infiltrated in the area of Baljkovica, more specifically into the Potocani [Realtime transcript read in error: "Potocari"] area. I cannot now be sure what time this was, but this was done at night. There are always some indications to this effect. There was increased artillery fire by the BH army on the Zvornik Brigade's area of responsibility. In our experience, they had not previously fired on both Zvornik and Kozluk, which are both far in the depth of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform the Chief of Staff of this intelligence?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where and how you informed Obrenovic of this intelligence.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall now whether I personally saw the Chief of Staff on the 14th. I think I did go down from Kula Grad to present the overall situation to him and all the potential threats I've been talking about. I am certain that I did get the information to him, whether orally or by courier, although I'm inclined to believe that I saw him myself either in the barracks or in the town or in the Snagovo area, which is most probable, that I went all the way there in order to present all this information to him. After this, I immediately returned to my post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification. Earlier the witness talked about the Potocani area where Naser Oric supposedly was about, and this is not Potocari as it's noted here. So the record is clear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. But the two words sounds, you know, familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the sake of the record, the witness said, "This is the area of Potocani," which is a village that is quite far from the town of Potocari. Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, would you tell me, please, when, at what time on the 14th of July this information could have reached the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The units were already coming into contact along the depth, starting with Velja Glava, as I said. Then there was information that there was contact in the area of the Bratunac Brigade, the Milici Brigade, and so on, and there was also intensified artillery fire. I think I received the information about the infiltration of Naser's group. I'm not sure whether it was in the night of the 13th to the 14th or maybe even the 14th to the 15th. The one thing I'm sure of is that this information was correct. And then I could have gone and reported in the morning hours, because I know that the infiltration was actually carried out after midnight, sometime early in the morning, 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning, so that I could have only seen Mr. Obrenovic before noon. I leave open the possibility that it might be some other time, but to the best of my recollection it was before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you sent all your intelligence information to the Chief of Staff as the focal point?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the evening of the 14th and the afternoon, was there any fighting? Were there any combat operations between the column and --

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening of the 14th, there was fierce fighting and for the first time there was an open conflict between the greater part of the column and the units of the Zvornik Brigade, the police units in the Maricice area, which is just below Kula Grad, the town -- the point where I was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point, the column was no longer concealed from the units of the army and police on the ground because that was when the direct contact took place. And it was really horrific. On both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the police a few times. Does this mean that at that point in the Maricice area there were also police units?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Kula area, in the direction of Mladjevac, which I've just mentioned. In this area, for the protection of Zvornik, this was where the first encounter took place with the police units. The police commander was captured by members of the head of the column of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, when you say "captured," you mean he was taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As an intelligence officer, did you learn about his imprisonment, and how did this come about?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him being taken prisoner with my own eyes from my vantage point, but I learned about it by means of radio surveillance. And this is how it happened: The capture of policeman Zoran Jankovic from the Doboj police force by a member of the BH army took place as follows: Zoran Jankovic tried to contact his superior. As his superior did not respond to his pleas, and he was saying, "Gavro, I've been taken prisoner. I'll be flayed alive. Please respond." And his voice left the impression of someone who had really been taken prisoner and was at someone else's mercy. As his superior did not respond, I responded using the signal of his superior. Obviously the BH army soldier who had taken him prisoner had taken his Motorola and he said, "Stop your fire. Otherwise, we will skin him alive. We will slaughter him. We'll kill him." I can't quote the words precisely. And I said to him, "Please don't do anything to him. We'll do our best to stop the fire." And I informed the Chief of Staff of this, probably using the other parallel line -- connection, and it was clear to everybody by then that there had been a clash of forces but the Chief of Staff obviously didn't know yet that the chief of police had been captured, the police commander, and I told him this. I said, "I have an open line to the man who is holding him. Let's try to negotiate about this," because the conflict was already -- the clash was already so close to the rear of our units that anyone with any military knowledge at all could see that there would be a blood-bath and that this could not end with casualties on only one side. Therefore, our assessment was that serious negotiations were called for, that there had to be a cease-fire and that the column had to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here for a moment. We are talking of the afternoon of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was already growing dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We have information that this is the period when Dragan Jokic was the duty operations officer of the Zvornik Brigade. Did you know this?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Did I know who was the duty operations officer? No, I didn't. And for my purposes, this was irrelevant. It was not my task to keep track of this. Nobody informed me of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We have information that in the area of the village of Orahovac in the afternoon of the 14th execution of the Muslim prisoners brought to the village of Orahovac started. Did you know anything about the arrival of these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it your task to look after these prisoners and to collect information about them in the depth of the territory of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No. Throughout my testimony, in the circumstances I am telling you about, I think it is quite evident that I was interested in the armed column moving along the Srebrenica-Tuzla axis. They were my priority. I had very little time to learn what was happening with the part of the column that was attempting to break through along the Srebrenica-Kladanj direction. I had very superficial information about this. My whole attention was focussed on what was happening at the head of the column and what was about to happen, what was happening in the units of the 241st, 242nd, 245th, 246th Brigades of the Tuzla Corps facing our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you know anything about the operations taking place in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this was the most fierce fighting that had taken place until that point. That was on the 14th in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: In my entire military career, this was the most fierce fighting in my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far was the location of these combat activities from the rear of the brigade -- the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies, it was not more than 3 or 3 and a half kilometres. Not as the crow flies, but along the terrain, for the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the Zvornik Brigade at the time facing the units of the 2nd Corps of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The composition of the Zvornik Brigade was as follows: There was a part of the units that I spoke about, the temporary units which were turned towards the column with whom were a part of the police units and a part of the military units were already in conflict with. Along the way the stationary part, its trenches were facing the members of the 2nd Tuzla Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We just wanted to clarify the military positions. Let us go back to the evening of the 14th. What happened with these captured -- with this captured police senior officer and was there a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The entire drama I followed, and I had very frequent communication with a member of the B and H army who was obviously holding this person. He even openly said that he will bring us to our target. This gave me hope that the police officer would survive. I had the situation where he would give the Motorola to Zoran Jankovic very often so that he could plead and he could request a cease-fire. But we had a problem. I had the problem, I who was insisting via the Chief of Staff for the fire to stop to all those to whom I could orally convey the request for a halt in the fire. The leader of that column obviously had the problem in the sense that it was already -- everything was in chaos and it was hard for anybody including the Chief of Staff at some point to halt the fire. Something happened which I found out about later, during the signing of the Dayton Peace Accords. I wanted to meet Zoran Jankovic, I did meet him, and he told me the entire dramatic situation, because he came out in 1996, and he told me about what had happened. A miracle had occurred. At the point where the leader had lost patience and had placed a knife on his throat, at that point the fire stopped. So that's how he survived. We did manage to stop the fire. Then it got dark. As soon as it got dark, it's difficult for the units on the ground and the members of the column and for the members of the police and the Zvornik military forces, which were facing the column, it was difficult; due to the circumstances, the night doesn't make it possible for the clashes to continue. It's more difficult to open fire. But I could imagine how afraid both sides were in such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, did the column manage to break through the first lines of defence? Did it manage to sever the road, the Zvornik-Zapardje road, and to go toward the units of the 2nd Corps of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Now I know that this high court and this institution cannot allow for assumptions, so at the moment I cannot answer that question, other than speak about the information which I knew at the time, and that was that the infiltrated group did manage to get into direct contact with the group and that there was a coordinated action by the units from the column and the units of the B and H army, belonging to the 2nd Corps, with increased pressure on the lines and increased pressure at the rear of the units so that already the next day, as you probably know yourself, there were certain negotiations and so on. However, I'm convinced that the line was broken through and that the agreement to open it was actually formalised later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you communicate with Dragan Obrenovic in the night between the 14th and the 15th via radio?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I most probably did, because I did have communication with him throughout that period. And if anything important was happening on the ground, I probably informed him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point did you find out that he personally was captured by members of the B and H army?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No. Other than seeing by the participants that he was in that Baljkovica region where all hell had broken loose. Other than that, I didn't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point you said that on the 15th negotiations began about opening the corridor for the passage of the column.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in these negotiations on the 15th in any way?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think a more precise answer would be that I participated in the mediation, because I was not a superior officer at that rank and it wasn't in accordance with my functional duty or my authorities. I was not one who could make decisions. However, on the 15th, I think 15th in the morning, I received information my listening group that Semso Muminovic, a member of the B and H army from the 2nd Tuzla Corps - I cannot remember his exact post at the time; I think that he was already doing intelligence duties and I think that he was a commander of one of the brigades. I can't remember which one any longer - he made a roll-call and he was looking for someone from the Army of Republika Srpska and from the Zvornik Brigade. I can't remember whether he wanted to actually speak to Vinko Pandurevic, but I received information at a certain frequency that he wanted to speak with someone, and I informed the Chief of Staff about this. I said that my listening post, my listening group, was picking up Mr. Muminovic's calls, and the Chief of Staff suggested that I should reply, and this is what I did. I responded to Mr. Muminovic's call, and we embarked on a dialogue about what was going on with the column and so on and so forth. He asked whether it was possible to reach an accord on opening the lines. I told him that "I will convey this information to my superiors," and the Chief of Staff then made a suggestion. He said that those conversations should be conducted at a certain pace, that I should impose such a pace of this conversation for as long as the main strength of the Zvornik Brigade forces needed to return to the area of responsibility that was theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a second there. Can you tell us at this point if you knew when did Commander Vinko Pandurevic return to the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to say whether this happened on the 14th in the afternoon or on the 15th in the afternoon. But I think, if the transcripts and the intercepts are speaking about this particular conversation and if it took place on the 15th, I only know that on the same day that I was in communication with Semso, that same afternoon I could see the units returning from Kula Grad back to the area of responsibility, because you could see the road leading back from Srebrenica-Drinjaca-Divcici [phoen] to Zvornik very well from that point where I was at, and I was at Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that at the point in time when you set off or began your communications with the other side, you could see Vinko Pandurevic? Does that mean that Vinko Pandurevic and the units he had taken to Srebrenica had not yet returned to the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The negotiations between myself and Mr. Muminovic lasted for quite a while, with breaks in between. We were creating an environment in which we could speak. We needed to achieve a truce first, and he gave word that he would do everything on his part to halt the artillery barrage, which was actually constant on the part of the B and H army. At the same time, I had to do my utmost to make sure that we halted our fire. I cannot state whether he was in a position to make decisions. I know that I conveyed this information immediately to the Chief of Staff, and then we would say, "Okay, let us now work on the truce," and then we would get back to each other in 15 minutes' time. So in this way both of us were trying to establish a normal environment in order to avoid what was actually starting to happen out on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your call sign at the time? How were you addressed in this radio traffic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: My usual signal or code-name was "Vuk," wolf. However, in those days, if the captured police officer called Gavro and Gavro did not respond, then I would respond as Gavro and speak on his behalf. If Semso Muminovic asked for the person and charge and no one responded, then I would respond on behalf of that person and say I was the person in charge. At one point, since Semso realised that I was not the person in charge and that I could not make any decisions, then I would say "Person X" and so on. So I would use "Vuk, "person in charge," "Glavni," "Gavro." But I did not do it in any situation and most often I responded as myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in this intensive radio communication during the intense combat operations on the 14th and the 15th you were representing yourself -- or introducing yourself under other names as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I can specifically say that I responded as wolf, "Vuk," as "X," or at the point when the police officer was requesting to speak to Gavro, I would say "Gavro," but not in any other circumstances. This happened maybe for three or four minutes, for very briefly I was the person in charge because Semso asked for the person in charge. And I would I would say, "I am in charge" in order to have the opportunity to have a conversation with him. I did not have any other call signs. Sometimes I would use the call sign "Ruka," hand, because I had been wounded in the hand, so for my soldiers from the listening group, because I also knew that others knew me as "Vuk," I would then for that reason change the name because the soldiers in the listening group would then tell that it was me. But these are the several signs that I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you falsely introduced yourselves at those times, in order to play tricks on the other side?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Allow me just to briefly deal with what has happened, because we will have other testimony about the combat operations, about the night of the 15th and the 16th and the 16th [as interpreted]. Could you please tell us what was happening on that night of combat between the 15th and the 16th. Was there a definite breakthrough? And what happened?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you now exactly what time it was. I cannot even establish the exact date when it was opened and when it was closed, because I no longer took part in that with the appearance of the Zvornik Brigade units. And once I received information received by the commander of the brigade, Mr. Pandurevic, from that point on, when he got the information that I had Semso Muminovic on the line -- and I did not communicate with him before that, because he wasn't in my line of sight and I had no communication with him -- on that afternoon - I think it was in the afternoon; maybe it was in the early evening - he called to this RUP-12 device and said, "Yes, I heard that you have Muminovic on the line." And then I passed that on to him. The frequency where Mr. Muminovic was was passed on to him. And from that point on their mutual agreement began about opening the line, and from that point on I no longer participated in this conversation. Of course, I could listen to it, but I didn't take part in it. I cannot remember when it was opened and when it was closed; however, I am still convinced that the line was already broken through and that it was only the official accord or the agreement whereby it was achieved that the line was opened from a certain point up to a certain point. Luckily, it was a probably a major thing that this happened at all, because I'm sure that with this action the number of casualties was reduced on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those days from the 13th to the 16th and the 17th, with the passage of the column, were captured members of the column appearing and did you communicate with those captured persons in order to gather intelligence data?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: One single captured person from that column with whom I talked - and I cannot remember the exact date when this took place, because with the opening of the corridor, I think that already on the 15th or 16th or the 17th, I think this was already on the 17th - that I had come down from Kula and I went to the forward command post and that's when I saw Pandurevic. I was still intensively working to try to pull out Zoran Jankovic, and since I already had information from the ground about the killings of our soldiers, about the -- also capture of our soldiers by this column, and specifically trying to pull out the son of a certain Dusan Gotovac. And in this sense, I am still in communication and even on that 17th - I think this was in the presence of Vinko and Dragan Obrenovic from the forward command post - we are in communication, it seems to me, except for Semso we then talked also with Mr. Malkic who was the commander of the 28th Division about the eventual release of Zoran Jankovic. And there were conversations at the time about the prisoners in the territory who at the time were already captured at Lisaca at a sector of the Masevica Brigade and so on and so forth. However, I'm coming back to your specific question. The only captured person from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina with whom I had spoken in the barracks, I don't know whether this was on the 17th or the 18th, maybe it was even on the 16th, but I think this was on the 17th or the 18th because by the 16th I practically -- no, not practically, I actually didn't go down there. So yes, it is Nedzad Ahmetovic, a communications person in the command of the 28th Division in Srebrenica. He was the personal communications officer of Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will come back to Nedzad Ahmetovic's statement, and we have will try to clarify that. We will go into more detail about your contacts with Nedzad Ahmetovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher now to show the witness Exhibit P121. For purposes of identification, this is Defence Exhibit 110. It's a collection of intercepts from Dekici and Nezuci. We had the testimony here of a person who took part in the listening-in of these conversations, and our witness today is also mentioned in these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, at one point today you said that you were aware of the fact that just as you were listening to the conversations of the B and H army, they were doing the same to you.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will now present to you a collection that the Prosecution has tendered, a collection of intercepts from the area of the 2nd Corps of the BH army, and I will ask you to briefly comment on those intercepts in which your then code-name is mentioned. Page ERN 0084-8949, on page 3 of the translation into English of this conversation. I have also provided this in B/C/S. That is the 13th of July, Thursday, Amazon 1 and Lovac 1: "Tell Vuk to call. The Chief is on his way towards you, and Vuk went past Amazon towards the base -- towards Amazon, towards the base." Amazon 1 replies, "Did Vuk tell you to go to the base?" Can you assist us by telling us who the participants are here. Who is Amazon 1 and who is Lovac or "hunter" 1?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: "Amazon" was usually used for tank drivers. I would say that this was an intercept that happened on the 13th in the morning when, let me remind you, I was with Mr. Obrenovic in the Snagovo area, and this was when I was leaving the area. I'm sure that "Amazon 1" is one of the tank crew. "Lovac 1" or "Hunter 1", I think this was the code name for Mr. Obrenovic, but on the short-wave when conversing with me he usually used the name "Avala." So this is probably an intercept from the radio centre of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If it says "the Chief is on his way towards you" and "Vuk went past Amazon towards the base," can you tell us in what direction they were moving? Each one of these.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: If "Amazon 1", if I went past Amazon from the area of Snagovo, according to my task for that day, I went to Kula. "Amazon 1" was obviously in the area of Snagovo and obviously -- or rather, it can be concluded that the chief was supposed to go to that area, the area of Snagovo. He was somewhere else, and he was on his way back to Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So he was on his way back to Snagovo?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there's logic in that. But it would be irresponsible to base facts on this segment of conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, I think the time is up for this morning's session, and I'm sorry that you did not finish your direct examination, but I believe that tomorrow morning you won't take much of a long time. Well, Witness, I'm afraid that you have to stay in The Hague for another day. As I did to other witnesses, that you are still under the oath, so do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we'll see you again tomorrow morning. The hearing is adjourned for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of July, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
